title: Gomez Lozano appointed to Governor’s Commission on Hispanic Affairs
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Gomez Lozano appointed to Governor’s Commission on Hispanic Affairs

 January 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 315
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Victoria Gomez Lozano, Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center's Hispanic outreach coordinator, was appointed to the Governor's Commission on Hispanic Affairs.Gomez Lozano, along with 23 other appointees, will bring both professional and cultural expertise to advise the administration on behalf of Maryland's Hispanic and Latino communities.
The appointment holds great weight for Gomez Lozano, a native of Mexico who moved to the United States about 16 years ago with her then-young daughter. Within her first two years in the country, she moved to Easton.
"It's very exciting for me as well, because it's a way to represent the Eastern Shore (and) the Hispanic community, which is our main goal, mission and focus in this center," she said. "So hopefully we can keep expanding this representation and working for the community."
For now, Gomez Lozano's focus on the commission is representation for the rural region and learning as she goes.
But in the future, she hopes to move forward policies to benefit Hispanic communities, which represent a fast-growing demographic in the state.
Growth in the Eastern Shore's Hispanic population is something Gomez Lozano and her colleagues at ChesMRC have seen in the 10 years since the nonprofit launched.
The organization served about 3,500 people last year, according to Matthew Peters, the center's executive director.
Locally, Gomez Lozano wants to promote awareness of the expanding Hispanic community's existence and the services ChesMRC provides for residents.
She has served as the center's Hispanic outreach coordinator for over six years — a job that's had her acting in multiple capacities as an interpreter, a notary and a certified application counselor for health insurance, among others. She is also a resource for first-generation college students and works with ChesMRC's development committee.
"If everybody's aware (of us), then we can always offer a more welcoming environment," Gomez Lozano said. "Because sometimes, even just visiting one agency can make a whole difference, just the way you receive and treat people."

title: Chestertown community, Washington College celebrate Martin Luther King Jr.
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Chestertown community, Washington College celebrate Martin Luther King Jr.

 January 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 656
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Although snow caused the cancellation of a march to celebrate and honor Martin Luther King Jr., the snow didn't stop people from attending the annual Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Breakfast and Banquet at Washington College for Martin Luther King Jr. Day on Monday.The event was put on by the MLK Joint Committee, which is made up of Minary's Dream Alliance, Chester Valley Ministers Association, Washington College Starr Center for the Study of the American Experience, the Kent County NAACP and Kent County Parks and Recreation.
Doncella Wilson, co-executive director of Minary's Dream Alliance, said a variety of community members — from elected officials to students — come out for this event every year.
"So it's a good representation of what the community truly looks like," she said.
The celebration kicked off with a breakfast at Hodson Hall Dining Hall. After that, attendees walked over to the Decker Theatre at the Gibson Center for the Arts on campus to hear speeches and watch performances.
The program opened with a reenactment of the Greensboro Four, a group of college students in North Carolina protesting segregation laws through staging a sit-in at the Woolworth's lunch counter.
Singing resounded through the theater at various times throughout the program, including a performance of "Lift Every Voice and Sing," often referred to as the Black National Anthem, by Amiya Potts and a performance by singer, songwriter and author Ty Bolden, singing her song "Free Woman."
Jamie "Mixx" Barrett was awarded the Commissioner William W. Pickrum Service Award.
Barrett, a graduate of Kent County High School and Maryland Barber School, owns Big Mixx's Beautiful Beginnings Unisex Salon. A member of the Kent County Local Management Board, mentor and licensed foster parent, Barrett serves his community in more ways than one.
Paul Tue III, co-executive director of Minary's Dream Alliance, said young people were infused throughout the program.
"And that's on purpose," he said.
Tue hosted a "barbershop conversation" during the program, with four Kent County High School students involved with Young Men Standing on Business. Tue asked the students questions about their takes on King's legacy.
Pat Nugent, the Miller Director of Civic Engagement at the Starr Center, said getting younger people involved helps to pass on the legacy.
"And that's really what the day is about," he said. "To infuse younger generations with a sense of civic duty and obligation, as well as to connect them to generations of folks who have been doing that in Kent County for decades."
The keynote speaker of the program, Jermichael Mitchell, a writer, philanthropist and community activist who ran for mayor of Salisbury this past year, talked about purpose.
"No matter what your age may be, young or old, every last one of us is born with a purpose," he said. "Every last one of us is born to do something in this world. And in order for us to live our dreams, we have to actually know that purpose and embody that purpose and move forward."
Mitchell talked about King "walking in his purpose" every day, no matter what he faced.
Shaila Parker, who attended the event said its important that King is recognized every year because he did so much to help unify people.
"(He) helped make sure everyone has access to different things, has rights, is respected, has dignity," she said.
Lisa Moody, who has been attending the event since 2017, said one thing special about Kent County is that when there is an event, the county comes out for it.
"So it's a great place to meet people or reunite with people," she said. "And of course with today being the MLK holiday, it's a good reason for us to all come together for a specific purpose."
Saturday, Jan. 20, at 3:30 p.m., the public is invited to back to Decker Theatre to watch the premiere of "Get on The Bus," a documentary that follows local students and community members take a journey from Chestertown to The Legacy Museum in Montgomery, Alabama to deliver historic materials.

title: Mid-Shore native appointed to Maryland Commission on African American History and Culture
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Mid-Shore native appointed to Maryland Commission on African American History and Culture

 January 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: News 
 
 715
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Jaelon Terrele Moaney has been appointed as a commissioner by Gov. Wes Moore to be on the Maryland Commission on African American History and Culture. His term is from 2023 to 2027.According to MCAAH website, the purpose of the "the commission is to identify and preserve buildings, communities and sites of historical and cultural importance to the African American experience in Maryland. This competitive program, offered once per year, is supported through an annual appropriation from the Maryland General Assembly and is administered as a joint partnership of the Maryland Commission on African American History and Culture and The Maryland Historical Trust."
They give away $5 million a year, and Moaney works with his commission to find suitable candidates who are either architecturally or culturally preserving Black history and identity.
"It is the first ever ethnic commission in the United States. It is something that our colleagues across the country look to as an example. I feel humble to join the group as the youngest. The commission, in general, documents, collects African American heritage across the state," said Moaney.
He covers Delmarva for the commission and currently lives in Cambridge with his wife. Moaney is a product of Talbot County Public Schools, where he played football. He went to Williams College in Massachusetts.
Moaney said he hopes to energize the commission.
"I am trying to expand notions of Blackness that center on joy, that center freedom, agency and maybe push and highlight elements of our culture here on the Shore that often get overlooked. I think we have to reinforce accurate portrayals of Black life as well as ones that normalize our culture," he said.
He takes a long historical look at how Black people have suffered in America.
"Our country is really trying to reconcile with wounds that haven't fully healed or even the past few weeks, some that are opening up scars that are deeper than we could imagine. Like the people of Haiti, who have a large population in Salisbury now, or the people who were elected in Federalsburg for the first time in centuries — have the space to give it justice," he said.
Moaney will bring the commission to Chestertown for a public meeting in April. That meeting will be in the Bethel AME Church, where the Freedom Riders came and stayed in 1962.
"We have regular commission meetings that will happen all over the state. It is a beauty to be at the sites we are trying to preserve. Some are trying to be restored, some have been restored, some are receiving grants," Moaney said.
"I was assigned two committees. One was African American Heritage Preservation Program. The funding for that just got raised by the assembly from $1 million to $5 million. Close to 50% of the awardees were on the Eastern Shore. It is a collaboration with the Maryland Historical Trust which is in the Department of Planning," he said.
Among the grants awarded by the commission through the Historical Preservation Program for fiscal year 2024 are:
$250,000 for the American Legion Mannie Scott Post 193 Building in Denton.
$138,000 to Alpha Genesis Community Development Corporation in Cambridge.
$200,000 to Kent County Public Library.
$250,000 to Bryan's United Methodist Church in Grasonville.
$250,000 to the Mid-Shore Community Foundation in Royal Oak.
The grants will offer assistance to organizations and private citizens in their sponsorship of projects involving the acquisition, construction, or improvement of sites related to African American heritage, according to a press release from the governor's office.
Moaney's other appointment is to the Inaugural Statewide Book Drive. "The best part are the oral histories. There are so many discoveries. It's a privilege to be there," he said.
Outside of his work on the commission, Moaney is the founder of literacy group called the Needle's Eye Academy.
"If you are familiar with Gil Scott-Heron. He was arguably the soundtrack to the Black power movement as a poet and a musician and an oralist. The song 'Needles Eye' is where the Academy's name emanates from. From the 1972 album 'Pieces of the Man,'" he said.
"They have been asking, 'Are there any college age students who will speak to high schoolers and maybe even start a book club. We donated our old book sales into Berkshire County Public Schools (Massachusetts). In August of 2020 we started online in Talbot County Public Schools with three wonderful students."

title: 'In Pursuit of Freedom' lecture at Kennard on Feb. 25
author: Staff Writer
content:
'In Pursuit of Freedom' lecture at Kennard on Feb. 25

 February 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 199
 Words 

 Read News Document

 St. Paul's Episcopal Church will present a Black History Month lecture at the Kennard African American Heritage Center in Centreville at 4 p.m. on Sunday, Feb. 25. The lecture, entitled "In Pursuit of Freedom" will be given by noted local historian Chris Pupke, a member of Kennard's Advisory Board and St. Paul's Church.The program will focus on the many ways that enslaved people in Queen Anne's County sought and fought for their freedom, including then use of the Underground Railroad, the taking up of arms, and litigation in the courts. There will be a question and answer period after the lecture.
Earlier, on the same day, noted baritone Thomas Beard will be singing two songs associated with the observance of Black History Month at the 10 a.m. service at St. Paul's. Included will be "Come Sunday" by Duke Ellington along with a classical selection.
Beard has performed at the White House and in the Washington National Opera's Young Artist Program, where he was the only African American personally chosen by maestro Placido Domingo to take part in the program. He also sung with many opera companies across the U.S.
St. Paul's Church is located at 301 S. Liberty Street in Centreville.

title: Cardin visits with Eastern Shore's Black watermen
author: COUNTRIBUTED
content:
Cardin visits with Eastern Shore's Black watermen

 February 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: COUNTRIBUTED | Section: Local News 
 
 333
 Words 

 Read News Document

 U.S. Sen. Ben Cardin hosted a roundtable discussion at Chesapeake College with several individuals featured in the Maryland Public Television documentary "Water's Edge: Black Watermen of the Chesapeake" and their families on Monday.Attendees included Dr. Cliff Coppersmith, Marc Castelli, Vera Meredith, Captain Tyrone Meredith, Kat De Shields-Moon, Dennis De Shields, Captain Marcus Wooley, Clayton Mitchell, Clayton Washington, Vincent Leggett and Edzel Turner.
This was an opportunity to better understand the plight of the Black waterman, their history on the Shore and determine what, if any role, the U.S. Government can play to help, Cardin's office said in a press release.
"From Western Maryland to the Eastern Shore, there are efforts across the state to preserve Black culture in Maryland. Each of these projects is important, but we need a coordinated effort to connect the dots to follow the history Black Marylanders including Black watermen. This is a story that needs to be more visibly told," Cardin said.
Part of the discussion included ways to publicly memorialize Maryland's Black watermen. The numbers of Eastern Shore Black watermen have gone from a couple hundred decades ago to less than 20.
The discussion also included designating more towns, like Oxford, as heritage sites and ports of memory for the transatlantic slave trade and connecting the sites across Maryland.
"The Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center in Centerville, Maryland, a place that's benefitting from the work Senator Cardin has done to restore and create that center, now heralds the history of Black watermen on the Eastern Shore," said Clayton Washington, president of Kennard Alumni Association. "We love telling these stories, and it's really important that we have the means to do it."
The meeting was part of a day-long tour of the Eastern Shore, in which Cardin met with various locals involved in agriculture and aquaculture. In addition to meeting with the watermen, Cardin participated in tours of Teddy Bear Fresh in Easton and TechOps in Stevensville and a roundtable discussion with representatives from the Shore's agriculture, aquaculture and environmental conservation communities.
